Consolidated guidelines emphasize the use of person-centered viral hepatitis strategic information to support the scale-up of prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services at the country level. 36. Meta-data tables outline recommended hepatitis indicators, including core and additional indicators, with detailed rationales for data collection, methods for obtaining numerator and denominator data, and potential disaggregation categories. 37. Disaggregated data are essential for identifying inequalities between subpopulations and tracking trends, with common categories including sex, age, HIV status, high-risk populations, and geographical location. 38. Age bands may vary between indicators, and smaller age bands are recommended in settings with robust electronic health information systems. 39. Disaggregation by key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals) should only be done when feasible and when data security and confidentiality can be ensured. 40. Core indicators typically use an unspecified reporting period and can be calculated over different timeframes to address program management questions at various levels. 41. Some indicators have specific reporting periods (e.g., the past 12 months) to reflect recommended service delivery guidelines or data collection methods. 42. Data should generally be recorded daily and reported quarterly at the national or subnational level. 43. The prevalence of chronic hepatitis B is measured by the number and proportion of people with HBsAg-positive serological status. 44. This indicator reflects the epidemic and service needs, serving as a numerator or denominator for other indicators along the result chain and cascade. 45. HBsAg is the biomarker for HBV infection, and its presence during a cross-sectional survey likely indicates chronic hepatitis B due to the low incidence of recent infections. 46. Analyzing the prevalence of chronic hepatitis B helps programs understand the burden of the disease and plan testing, care, and treatment accordingly. 47. The prevalence of chronic hepatitis C is measured by the number and proportion of people with HCV RNA-positive or HCV core antigen-positive status. 48. This indicator reflects the epidemic and service needs, serving as a numerator or denominator for other indicators along the result chain and cascade. 49. Anti-HCV antibodies indicate past or present HCV infection but do not distinguish between resolved or active infection. 50. Recommended biomarkers for chronic hepatitis C include HCV RNA and HCV core antigen. 51. Analyzing the prevalence of chronic hepatitis C helps programs understand the burden of the disease and plan testing, care, and treatment accordingly. 52. The availability and readiness of HBV and HCV drugs and diagnostics are measured by the extent to which resources and conditions are in place to provide services according to defined minimum standards. 53. Service readiness includes the presence and functionality of basic amenities, trained staff, guidelines, equipment, diagnostics, and medicines. 54. Service availability refers to the physical presence of services, such as infrastructure, staff, and beds, as well as the availability of specific services in facilities. 55. The percentage of facilities offering HBV birth-dose vaccination, onsite testing for hepatitis B and C, and antiviral therapy for hepatitis B and C is assessed. 56. Trends in the availability of laboratory services for viral hepatitis B and C testing are measured to ensure sufficient capacity for testing and treatment. 57. The coverage of timely hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination is measured by the proportion of newborns receiving the vaccine within 24 hours of birth. 58. This indicator reflects access to vaccination at birth and progress toward eliminating vertical transmission of HBV. 59. Disaggregation of data by age, place of birth and residence, sex, and socioeconomic status is recommended. 60. Global reporting platforms include the WHO Global Hepatitis Reporting System and the WHO/UNICEF joint reporting form.
